knownFor.label: Sputnik & Gagarin
knownFor.note: First satellite (1957) and first human in space (1961).

knownFor.label: AK-47 rifle
knownFor.note: The most widely produced assault rifle in history.

knownFor.label: Five-Year Plans
knownFor.note: State planning of the whole economy.

location.value: The largest country by area (22.4 million km²), spanning Eastern Europe and northern and Central Asia across 11 time zones, and bordering twelve countries.

terrain.value: Plains, taiga, tundra, steppe and deserts, with the Ural and Caucasus mountains and great rivers.

climate.value: Mostly cold continental. Harsh conditions hampered agriculture.

resources.value: Oil and gas, coal, iron, gold, timber and farmland.

disasters.value: Forced collectivisation contributed to a devastating famine in 1930–1933 that killed millions, especially in Ukraine and Kazakhstan. In Ukraine it is known as the Holodomor, which many countries recognise as genocide, a characterisation some historians debate. Later disasters included Chernobyl (1986) and the shrinking Aral Sea.

population.value: 286,730,819 in the 1989 census, the world’s third most populous country.

urbanisation.value: Rapid urbanisation through forced industrialisation. Moscow was the capital and largest city.

disease.value: Health improved after the 1920s, but life expectancy stagnated in the 1970s–80s.

migration.value: Mass deportations of peoples (e.g. Chechens, Crimean Tatars, Volga Germans) and the Gulag forced labour camp system. Peasants moved to cities.

economicBase.value: A centrally planned economy: state-owned industry, five-year plans from 1928, and collectivised agriculture.

tradeRoutes.value: Trade mainly within the socialist bloc (Comecon). Oil and gas exports to the West from the 1970s.

wealth.value: The second-largest economy in the world for much of its history. GDP (PPP) about $2.66 trillion ($9,211 per person) in 1989 (Wikipedia infobox).

moneyAndTax.value: The Soviet ruble, with state-set prices. Shortages and hidden inflation grew in the 1980s.

inequality.value: Low income inequality (Gini 27.5 in 1989), but party officials (the nomenklatura) had special privileges.

governmentType.value: A federal communist one-party state governed by the Communist Party under Marxism–Leninism, through councils (soviets).

keyRulers.value: Lenin (1922–1924). Stalin (the “undisputed personalist ruler” from about 1929 to 1953). Khrushchev (de-Stalinisation). Brezhnev (1964–1982). Gorbachev (1985–1991).

succession.value: No formal succession rule. Leaders emerged from power struggles in the party leadership (e.g. after Lenin’s death in 1924).

institutions.value: The Communist Party, the Politburo, the Supreme Soviet (1936–1991), the secret police (Cheka, NKVD, KGB) and central planning (Gosplan).

stability.value: Stalin’s Great Purge (late 1930s): mass arrests, executions and show trials. Totalitarian rule, then the reforms and crises of the late 1980s.

eliteConflict.value: Power struggles after Lenin and Stalin. Khrushchev was ousted in 1964. A failed hardliner coup took place in August 1991.

armyAndTech.value: The largest standing military and the largest nuclear arsenal of the Cold War era.

majorWars.value: The Russian Civil War (before 1922). The Second World War (the “Great Patriotic War”, 1941–45), with around 27 million deaths, the most of any country. The Soviet–Afghan War (1979–89).

territoryChange.value: Annexed the Baltic states and parts of Poland, Finland and Romania (1939–40). After 1945 it dominated Eastern Europe through satellite states and the Warsaw Pact (1955).

alliancesRivals.value: The Molotov–Ribbentrop pact with Nazi Germany (1939), then the Allies against Germany. The Cold War rivalry with the US and NATO. The Sino-Soviet split.

inventions.value: Space Race firsts: Sputnik 1, the first satellite (1957), and Yuri Gagarin, the first human in space (1961). Nuclear power and weapons.

scienceEducation.value: Mass literacy campaigns and free education, and strong science and engineering. Some fields were held back by ideology (e.g. Lysenko’s influence on biology).

openness.value: Closed to outside ideas and travel for most of its history. Glasnost (openness) from 1985 allowed freer debate.

communicationTransport.value: The Moscow Metro, whose first 13 stations opened on 15 May 1935.
communicationTransport.source: Mos.ru, Moscow city transport news (checked 10 Nov 2026)

religion.value: A secular state with official state atheism. Religious institutions were repressed, especially in the 1920s–30s.

languageWriting.value: Russian (official), plus the languages of the 15 republics (Ukrainian, Kazakh, Georgian and others).

artsArchitecture.value: Socialist realism (the official style). Composers Shostakovich and Prokofiev. Writers such as Pasternak and Solzhenitsyn, who faced censorship.

socialStructure.value: Officially classless, but with a privileged party elite. Collective farmers, industrial workers, and millions of Gulag prisoners.

sharedIdentity.value: A “Soviet” identity promoted alongside national republics. Motto: “Workers of the world, unite!”

dailyLife.value: Shared communal apartments, later small prefabricated flats (khrushchyovka); bread, potatoes, cabbage; queues for goods.

neighbours.value: Twelve neighbours, including Finland, Poland, Romania, Turkey, Iran, Afghanistan, China, Mongolia, North Korea and Norway.

ideasReligions.value: Spread communism and supported revolutionary movements worldwide (China, Cuba, Vietnam, and anti-colonial movements).

colonisation.value: Not a colonial empire in the formal sense, but it dominated non-Russian republics and Eastern European satellite states and put down uprisings there (East Germany 1953, Hungary 1956, Czechoslovakia 1968).

riseSignals.value: The October Revolution (1917), victory in the Civil War, and rapid industrialisation under the five-year plans. Victory in the Second World War made it a superpower.

peakPeriod.value: From the 1950s to the 1970s, the era of superpower status and space achievements.

declineSignals.value: Economic stagnation under Brezhnev, the costs of the arms race and the Afghan war, nationalist movements, and the 1991 coup attempt.

outcome.value: Dissolution. The Soviet Union formally dissolved on 26 December 1991 into 15 independent states. Russia became its successor state (taking its UN seat), and most republics joined the CIS.

sources.value: Soviet archives (opened after 1991), censuses, official statistics (sometimes unreliable), and memoirs. Checked against Wikipedia on 5 Nov 2026. See also Suny (2011).

overallCertainty.value: Good for structure and events. Death tolls from repression, famine and war vary by source, and Soviet economic statistics are debated.
